items.title: 2035 came early
items.content:
tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox .

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript.

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev .

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev .

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package , over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability.

I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix .

It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm , 1 1 With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster.  especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload. 2 2 The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland , and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl , git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay. 3 3 Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix , and it loading trynix.dev , and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 4 4 Do not be too overjoyed. It took more than an hour for this to render.

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

items.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
items.content:
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?

Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.

So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.

It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks

Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.

So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone ???

This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp [1] , but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!

Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.

Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important…

items.title: Security incident on Hex.pm
items.content:
On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability.

We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs.

Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm . Please forward suspicious emails to security@hex.pm .

We checked every file written to package storage during the incident against our database and found nothing unexpected. Reads of private packages in that period came from our own servers and coincide with releases the same organizations published at the time. A read made from a compromised server would look like one of ours, so we can't fully rule one out, and reads of private documentation aren't logged. We will contact affected organizations directly.

The attacker's commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients. We're building a new registry signing system that supports key rotation, with new Hex client releases in the coming days. Until then, don't trust third-party mirrors and fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm. We already deployed fixes for the vulnerability and are working on further hardening fixes.

Reset your 2FA at hex.pm/dashboard/security : under "Authenticator App", choose "Setup New App" and verify a code from the new entry. You get a new secret and new recovery codes, so store the new codes. This works when an organization requires 2FA, where disabling it is refused.

Update your Hex client when the release with the new signing system is out in the coming days. Until then, use only repo.hex.pm, not mirrors. To update, run mix local.hex --force , and update rebar3 or Gleam if you use them.

18:16 - 18:29 : The attacker sent 69 malicious requests to hex.pm, six of our web servers were affected. Our error tracker Sentry recorded its first error at 18:16:00 and recorded an error for each request.

18:27 : We added a firewall rule to block the attacker's traffic, which took full effect between 18:30 and 18:33.

18:30 - 18:31 : All hex.pm servers were replaced with a patched build that rejects these payloads.

18:33 - 18:38 : All further requests from the attacking address were denied.

18:35 : We began investigating production logs and the database.

18:49 : We deactivated the AWS access key the affected servers used, after creating a replacement at 18:47.

19:07 : We received an email with a security report that described the same vulnerability.

20:21 : Most infrastructure credentials were rotated. The database password followed on November 24.

22:58 : We reported a personal data breach to IMY, the Swedish data protection authority.

23:05 : We reported the incident to CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which confirmed receipt at 23:43.

23:26 : We submitted an early warning to ENISA, the EU Agency for Cybersecurity.

By 10:42 : We had rotated every credential the attacker could have read, including the database password, except the registry signing key and a few low-impact secrets.

The vulnerability in Hex.pm is tracked as CVE-2026-129514 .

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.content:
Tidal is banning fully AI-generated music from its platform

Alexandra Mae Jones | CBC News | Posted: November 24, 2026 8:53 PM | Last Updated: 2 hours ago

Any fully AI-generated track will be rejected and removed from the platform as of Dec. 9, the company says

Caption: A woman walks with headphones on in New York. Streaming platform Tidal said Tuesday that as of Dec. 9, 'any wholly AI-generated track that's submitted to Tidal will be rejected and removed from our platform.' (Andres Kudacki/Reuters)

Tidal announced Tuesday it is banning fully AI-generated music from its streaming platform, in an update to its earlier policies aiming to protect musicians.

As of Dec. 9, "any wholly AI-generated track that’s submitted to Tidal will be rejected and removed from our platform," the company said in a statement .

"To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we're removing all tracks that we determine are 100 per cent AI generated."

Tracks made with the assistance of AI will still be permitted.

Earlier this year, Tidal introduced an AI policy to clearly tag and demonetize AI-generated music, as well as a crackdown on AI-generated impersonations of artists.

Tidal's latest move to ban fully AI tracks comes amid an influx of AI-generated songs being submitted to the platform — songs that no one is listening to, the company says.

"Yet Tidal subscribers are not listening to these tracks: 96 per cent of them have received zero streams in the last three months," the company said.

"It's true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fan bases. But this situation is different — at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried."

items.title: Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native
items.content:
Bypassing iOS Safari’s 60 FPS Limit to Build Web Applications That Feel Native

Rida F'kih · November 20, 2026 · 10 min read

Devon Govett of React Aria posted “Scrolling is All You Need: Building a Swipeable Sheet” back in October, and in it he talked about his team developing a sheet component that cleverly leverages the physics and smooth interactions provided by native browsers to provide the illusion of a native interaction.

More recently, Jordan Walke , creator of React, posted a video of an experiment on X showing a convincing native-like mobile interaction using DOM & CSS. It re-established a long-lived itch that I’ve had, and prompted this response from me. It’s something I could never justify building, however. Anything I built using this method would be pegged to 60 FPS.

What the video Jordan Walke posted doesn’t show is that, unless you flip the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” flag buried deep within the Safari developer settings on iOS, WebKit limits requestAnimationFrame to just 60 Hz on a 120 Hz screen, and on a regular page, touch and pointer events are held to that same rate. This is what makes even the best mobile websites feel irritating to use.

How can I make this experience suck less without resorting to flags? Let’s call back to the React Aria piece. The reason it feels so nice is that scrolling is the responsibility of the compositor. It runs in its own thread. It moves, clips and fades without a JavaScript round-trip.

Finger to digitizer, digitizer to compositor, compositor to GPU. This will become the basis of our interaction.

Behold, two grids. They both move a square when you drag. The one on the left uses JavaScript events and sets the transform attribute in CSS, while the one on the right simply places a square in a scrollable area.

If you’re on iOS Safari, you’ll immediately be able to tell which is which because one refreshes at most 60 times a second in a renderer pass, while the other uses the compositor.

In order to leverage the power of the scroll area, we need to find a way to read the scroll position outside of the renderer. If we can do that, we can treat it like a trackpad, or use it to “extract” native bounce, physics, momentum, etc., and apply them directly from the compositor to our animations.

Want a 1:1 trackpad experience? We just measure only when the finger is pressed.

Want a true trackball with native momentum? We just make it an infinitely scrollable region.

Want native bounce? We configure over-scroll padding and set the bounds of the container.

The point is, it’d be crazy flexible if we could just find a way to pull the values out of it frequently enough.

I measured scroll events updating 5 to 26 times per second during momentum scroll on an iPhone Duo. The best-case scenario is during slow, deliberate scrolls where it reaches almost 60 updates a second. Useless.

Instead, we’ll be aiming to read scrollTop and scrollLeft synchronously.

First, I tried having a MessageChannel call itself recursively, which worked: but it produced 50,000 reads a second with just 80 distinct values. That’s a lot of waste and heat since it pins a CPU core.

Next failure was trying to use Atomics to wake at the screen’s refresh rate, which worked and similarly extracted 80 distinct positions every second, but the drawbacks were too great. items.title: Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France
items.content:
Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French users. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond quickly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours.

We are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see our announcement of this deactivation from one month ago.

We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Currently, the courts have upheld beIn’s demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties.

We have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and counter-productive effort , but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines.

This is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: users who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9.

We object to the core premise of the legal arguments, which is the false assertion that recursive DNS can or should be used as a method to prevent piracy or any other type of content access. items.title: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found 17 unreported bugs
items.content:
I read Koukyosyumei's article " 著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話 " (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs").

The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain.

Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples.

I checked the collections with differential testing against the java.util collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org.

They include reduce on vector-of , the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries.

The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as = and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21.

The links to the source point to the clojure-1.12.7 tag.

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition.

You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32 , the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations.

So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of % .

When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code.

I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property.

Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results.

For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

For vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level.

The operations were conj , pop , assoc , and their transient versions.

I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before.

I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays.

Clojure implements it in gvec.clj , written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector .

If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65504 ))))

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65505 ))))

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( vec ( range 65505 ))))

The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj , where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

( recur result ( bit-and 0xffe0 ( + aidx 32 )))

The code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it.

With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504.

After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce .

items.title: More predictable notifications on GitHub.com
items.content:
Starting December 1, 2026, we’re migrating notifications on GitHub.com over the course of a week to make subscriptions more predictable, correct unexpected behavior, and support the growing scale of activity.

During the rollout, notifications may behave differently for different users. No action is required, but the changes below may affect how you manage and filter notifications. This does not apply to GitHub Enterprise Server.

Routine activity won’t resubscribe you: Previously, after manually unsubscribing, notification activities such as commenting, submitting a pull request review, changing a thread’s state, or merge queue activity resulted in a re-subscription. Now, those actions leave you unsubscribed. Being mentioned, assigned, or receiving a pull request review request will continue to resubscribe you since those actions ask for your attention.

Team-mention notifications will reflect current team membership and mentions: Previously, you could continue receiving notifications after a team mention was removed or you left the team. If you joined a team after it was mentioned, you wouldn’t receive notifications for future activity. Now, removing the mention or leaving the team stops future notifications based on that team mention, so you may receive fewer notifications. Joining the team enables notifications for future activity on threads where it was already mentioned. Other reasons, such as commenting, may still result in notifications.

Removing a mention won’t stop notifications you receive for other reasons: Previously, removing a mention could stop notifications even if you’d also participated in another way. Now, if someone removes a mention, you’ll stay subscribed as long as another reason, such as commenting or being assigned, still applies.

The Subscriptions page will show only subscriptions you added manually : The Subscriptions page will only list threads you explicitly subscribed to, not threads you get notifications for because you authored, commented, were assigned, were mentioned, or were asked to review. To manage those notifications and bulk-unsubscribe, use your notification inbox .

Notification reasons will follow a consistent priority: The reason shown in your inbox and email footer is now based on priority instead of the most recent activity. The order is mention, team mention, assign, review requested, comment, manual, author, state change, and subscribed. For issues, assign has the highest priority. If you filter or automate based on notification reasons, review those rules, since the reason shown may change.

Email headers will include all notification reasons: Notification email headers will include all applicable notification reasons, such as “mention” and “subscribed”, helping you better filter notifications. If you use filters or automations based on these notification reasons, please review them as they will now include all notification reasons.

Team mentions in security advisory comments will show a “team mention” reason: If your team is @mentioned in a comment on a repository security advisory, the notification will say “team mention” instead of “commented”.

Other notification behaviors, such as notification settings, watched repositories, custom thread subscriptions, and previously delivered notifications remain unchanged.

An illustrated celebration of the engineering around us

When I first started designing this site, I would constantly look around my home for objects that I had never given a second thought. Two products stood out to me as wonderfully mechanical and common: the mechanical pencil and the spray bottle.

The modern spray bottle emerged in the early 1970s, and by now there must be hundreds, maybe even thousands, of spray bottle designs out there in the world, with variations on their nozzle design, trigger mechanism and more. But they all utilize the same basic one-way-valve mechanism.

The main question we want to answer: How does fluid keep spraying out, pull after pull, every time you squeeze the Trigger? Let's get into it!

items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reportedly Had at Least 4 Affairs
items.content:
Quantifying some business guy’s sex life may not be classy work, but newly reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs have the power to move trillions of dollars in shareholder value around. To paraphrase New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , this guy’s libido determines whether or not a lot of people will ever get to retire, so we all deserve to know how many affairs there were.

And the answer, according to the Wall Street Journal’s latest anonymously sourced report on the AI chip company, is at least four . At least .

During an hours-long meeting of the Nvidia board on Sunday, the Journal writes, Huang told the board about “additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported.” The report is attributed to “people with knowledge of the discussion.”

Three alleged affairs have been widely reported . Huang has publicly acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, who is alleged to have been spying on behalf of the Chinese government , but there were two other alleged relationships with Nvidia employees as well. At any rate, whatever the Journal’s report considers “additional affairs beyond the two,” the use of the plural “affairs” means the board has heard about four at minimum.

Huang resigned on November 12 , then for over a week, tech stocks teetered , and then amid an SEC probe of Nvidia, plunged on Friday , sparking fears that the AI bubble had officially burst .

President Trump, a personal friend of Huang’s, has insisted that Huang did “ nothing wrong .” Trump did, however, post a meme on Truth Social on Monday—shortly after Huang’s reinstatement—showing a bloodied Huang posed with his fist in the air like Trump after his 2024 assassination attempt, holding aloft a bra .

On Monday, after Huang’s return, Nvidia gained back $990 billion in market value , reportedly the largest single-day gain for a U.S. company in history.

The Journal’s report says Huang was contrite about the additional affairs. During a speech to employees on Monday, he thanked them and told them he would be a “better CEO the second time around.”

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Hexagonal minesweeper - Hexsweeper
items.content:
The sphere keeps its depth and numbers while you turn it. After a mine, one Undo button takes the move back; New sphere starts over.

It's minesweeper on a ball of hexagons, so there are no edges or corners to hide behind. Tap a face to clear it and hold to flag it; the first clear is always safe. Drag to spin the sphere, pinch to zoom.

* Five sizes, from a quick 162 faces to a 2,252-face slog, with your best time kept for each.

* Undo. One bad tap doesn't have to end the run. Undo, New sphere and Flag sit in a small bar; everything else is behind ?.

* Light and Dark looks, plus the live materials Mercury and Aurora. The direct download adds three photo themes.

* It waits for you. Close the app mid-game and the board is there when you come back.

* Something hidden: hold the mine count at the top, and keep holding.

The phone app is the sphere only. The web version at https://dr.eamer.dev/games/hexsweeper/ adds Infinite, an endless plate, and Classic, a fixed board.

No account, no ads, no analytics, no tracking. The app makes no network requests and doesn't ask for internet access: the game, fonts and pictures are all inside. Your board, best times and settings are saved on the device. Android backup can carry best times, theme and settings to a new phone; the unfinished board stays on the device.

Needs Android 7.0 or later on a phone or tablet with a touchscreen.

items.title: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers
items.content:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.

We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500 .

2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.

Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested

2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.

Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie

Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.

2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.

2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.

Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server.

Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine.

The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.

items.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
items.content:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.

I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)

Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.

Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: The Tech Workers Movement is a global political actor
items.content:
Tech Workers are spearheading the global initiative Down with Data Centers, a weekend of action against Big Tech that will take place on the 23rd and 24th of January.

The initiative is a big tent designed to show the world how much the forceful and rushed deployment of technologies nobody asked for is despised by communities, workers, and citizens. Hyperscalers data centers are the symptom, and as tech workers, we know the wasteful expense of electricity, water, land, and the disrespect towards local communities are not technical problems. They are embedded in the very logic of the industry, because it’s the same logic applied to our own well-being in the workplace. The careless and abusive way companies build data centers embodies the same attitude they push on us to build what we work on: cutting corners, disregarding laws, and ignoring the people impacted.

Hyperscalers and the surplus of “cheap” computation they provide do not benefit workers. They do not benefit those who live next to them. They do not benefit the victims of military aggression orchestrated through the increasingly automated kill chains. They do not benefit the environment, and they are for sure not necessary to run imaging software to detect cancer. They do not benefit the netizens, who are being flooded with endless waves of slop. They do not benefit the surveilled activists and organizers, targeted by state repression.

The world, in the last few years, has been waking up to the relevance of technology for politics, society, and individual and collective well-being. We have known this for a while, because we are at the front lines where these technologies are conceived, designed, and implemented. We see the trends before others, because many of us sit in the same rooms with the people who want or enable the technological system we live in.

Imagine if your coked-out boss who can’t edit an Excel file had the power to influence the economic policies around technology for half of the world, or advise top politicians on how to put LLMs in a system that controls nuclear warheads. Well, it happened to some of us.

It is no surprise, then, that tech workers are at the forefront of such an initiative. Tech Workers Coalition (TWC), WhatWeWill (WWW), United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW), and Computer Professional Union (CPU) are just some of the unions and tech workers’ collectives actively preparing actions.

Down with Data Centers is just a weekend of action. It will create relationships. It will mobilize people, and some of them will stay active throughout. Protest alone doesn’t change things, though. Every organization joins the initiative from a different strategic position and hopes to benefit from this concerted effort.

For tech workers specifically, though, this represents a special occasion. While international organizing is understood as a necessity since the tech industry is far-reaching, the concrete chances to put this consensus into practice. Sure, there have been coordinated strikes or protests in specific companies across countries, but these efforts could only involve tech unions, and only the ones already active in those companies.

This time it is different: the frame of Down with Data Centers allows local initiatives and different types of organizations to apply political pressure to different points of leverage, depending on their context. Therefore, different types of tech unions, tech workers’ collectives, and movements involving a large number of tech workers can finally present themselves on the stage of global politics as a relevant, coherent political actor.

A timely occasion, fit to overcome the now stale narrative that tech workers taking a political stance or organizing in the workplace are exceptional, novel, and curious happenings. Now that technology is at the center of politics, politics should become a central aspect of tech workers’ identity.

items.content:
My first two Mac apps, Front and Center and SwitchGlass , were both created back in 2020 to restore features from DragThing , the venerable Mac app that was retired in 2019. The one tiny feature that Front and Center provided was literally a single checkbox within DragThing’s preferences. SwitchGlass went a bit farther, recreating one specific kind of floating palette from DragThing ( and classic Mac OS ).

After 24 years of development, DragThing had a ton of features. People often joked that I was destined to slowly reimplement all of DragThing’s functionality in a series of small apps. Put another way, they were saying I was doomed to make strange little Mac apps with extremely limited appeal (and sales).

Perhaps to prove them wrong, the next app I created was Hyperspace , which provided a way to reclaim disk space without removing any files . Hyperspace was still a nerdy app, but at least it had somewhat broader appeal than my earlier efforts. Who doesn’t want to save disk space? But more importantly, it was totally unrelated to DragThing. I had broken the curse!

Alas, there was one more (small) thing from DragThing that I missed. I used to have a DragThing palette in the corner of my screen containing some commonly used folders. In earlier versions of macOS, it was possible to pin the Dock to a screen corner, but that wasn’t really what I wanted either. I just wanted a small, separate palette of folders in the corner.

This is not a hard problem to solve. Plenty of Mac apps can provide something close to what I want…but not exactly what I want, in the specific way that I want it . For many years, I got by with some folders in the corner of my desktop. But the problem nagged at me.

A few years ago, I went so far as to implement my desired feature in SwitchGlass , adding the ability to create a small, extra palette full of folders in addition to the app switcher. But it felt incongruous with the rest of the app, so I never shipped it. And I didn’t want to maintain my own private fork of SwitchGlass, so I abandoned that branch of the code.

Today, AI coding agents are helping to produce a bounty of new , niche Mac apps, many made by people who have little or no coding experience. Even for experienced software developers, vibe coding has made it possible to create apps that were previously “not worth building” due to an unfavorable ratio of effort to payoff.

It’s in this context that I revisited my “little palette of folders” idea. Surely I could vibe-code a simple app just for me in a day or two, right?

So what happened? The well-known programmer’s credo comes to mind: “We do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy.” Indeed.

I began the project by feeding a coding agent the source code to my app, SwitchGlass , as a starting point. I wrote SwitchGlass six years ago using a substantially more primitive version of SwiftUI. (For the developers out there, it predates @Observable and @State , and it supports Macs all the way back to macOS 12 Monterey from 2021.) I asked a coding agent to modernize the code and generalize it to support an arbitrary number of palettes instead of just one app switcher palette per display.

It worked, and quickly! But it was pretty shoddy. Many optimizations and niceties from SwitchGlass had been lost. So I dove in to fix them…and maybe add one or two more features, I guess…

Now, after months of work, I’ve created a bit of a monster. But in the process, I’ve fulfilled a long-held dream of mine—a dream I had set aside years ago because I thought it was impossible. I’ve replaced the Dock.

If you’ve read any of my Mac OS X reviews , you know that I’ve always been dissatisfied with the Dock. Over the past couple of decades, I’ve gotten used to it, but I still bump up against its limitations and undesirable behaviors every day. (Undesirable to me, anyway.)

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. items.title: GrapheneOS shows off how it plans RCS support without Google Messages
items.content:
RCS is coming to GrapheneOS without Google Messages, as a proof-of-concept app shows how the privacy-focused version Android can implement the messaging standard.

As virtually all Android phones and now iPhone support RCS messaging, the standard is key to communication in 2026. But GrapheneOS users, by default, are still stuck with SMS/MMS as RCS is typically locked behind Google Messages on Android.

It’s a problem that Graphene’s developers have been trying to work out for a while now, and it seems progress is being made. A proof-of-concept messaging app with RCS was shared on Twitter/X, showing Graphene’s RCS implementation working with both Google Messages and iOS with end-to-end encryption and full features including typing indicators and reactions.

While this app skips the need to use Google Messages directly, the app does still use Google’s services as most carriers rely on Google for RCS. GrapheneOS still needs a sandboxed version of Google Play, for now, for this to work, but the developers say that a standalone version for carriers that support Google-less RCS will be coming.

We made a proof of concept RCS messaging app. It already has end-to-end encryption with MLS compatible with Google Messages and iOS, typing indicators, delivery/read receipts, reactions and media/file sharing. We'll use what was learned to integrate RCS into our Messaging app. pic.twitter.com/jzCTCCKrIQ

There’s still no firm timeline for this new RCS support on GrapheneOS, but Google Messages can still be used in the meantime.

items.title: OpenProject wins multimillion-dollar contract from ITZBund to replace Jira
items.content:
ITZBund, the IT service provider for Germany’s federal administration, has signed a new framework agreement with the open-source Jira alternative OpenProject. The Berlin-based software company will provide an open-source issue-tracking solution to replace existing Atlassian Jira environments. The contract includes migration services, training, support and further development of the platform. The issue tracker is a separate lot in a tender for ITZBund’s cloud-based software development and project management platform.

According to the contract award notice , the agreement runs for four years and covers up to 1,450 instances and 150,776 person-hours. The notice does not give specific financial details; OpenProject told iX that the contract is worth eight figures. The tender also explicitly aimed to strengthen digital sovereignty by having ITZBund procure more open-source tools.

Jira Data Center to be discontinued in 2029

Niels Lindenthal, co-founder and CEO of OpenProject GmbH, said: “The award is a major milestone for OpenProject and a strong signal for the European open-source community.” OpenProject says it sees more and more companies and public institutions questioning their dependence on proprietary software platforms. The company also emphasizes that recent versions have significantly expanded OpenProject’s migration features to make it easier for organizations to move away from Jira.

In this case, Atlassian’s announcement that it will discontinue the on-premises version of Jira Data Center in March 2029 may also have prompted the tender. The phaseout is gradual: only existing customers can purchase new licenses through March 30, 2028. Atlassian said it was taking this step because nearly all new customers now choose the cloud.

items.title: What VP != VNP Means (In 3 Minutes)
items.content:
I assume you know about the P vs. NP problem. But what is this wacky thing Anthropic just posted ?

You learned how to take a determinant in your linear algebra class:

det ( 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 ) = 1 ⋅ ( 5 ⋅ 9 - 6 ⋅ 8 ) - 2 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 9 - 6 ⋅ 7 ) + 3 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 8 - 5 ⋅ 7 ) = 0 The naive way is fine for 3 × 3 matrices, but notice that you need to perform Θ ( n ! ) arithmetic operations here. Exercise for the reader is to find the exact number of operations (hint: start with a recurrence relation).

Luckily, if you paid attention, you will remember there are faster ways to do this for big n × n matrices, like Gaussian elimination. If we stick only to adding and multiplying, we can still find a determinant in polynomial time ( there are better ways, but this is an old, readable method ).

A related problem to the determinant is finding the permanent. It’s like a determinant without any subtraction:

perm ( 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 ) = 1 ⋅ ( 5 ⋅ 9 + 6 ⋅ 8 ) + 2 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 9 + 6 ⋅ 7 ) + 3 ⋅ ( 4 ⋅ 8 + 5 ⋅ 7 ) = 450 Unlike determinants, there is no known way to compute permanents in polynomial time. Since finding the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s is NP-hard (and in fact #P-complete ), it would be pretty important if there were a way.

What the Anthropic proof that VP ≠ VNP means is that there is no way to do this if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size, which look like this:

This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn’t clear how they would help with the permanent. If you think of a way, go claim your $1 million.

items.title: GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'
items.content:
GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'

1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Joe Tidy Cyber correspondent, World Service, Woolwich Crown Court

During the trial, the prosecution described Kurtaj as a "leading light" in the teen gang Lapsus$

A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.

Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."

The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.

Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.

He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.

City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".

He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.

He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

GTA 6 was released to much fanfare last week

The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.

Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.8m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.

The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

When he was sentenced he stood and smiled.

He had short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt without a tie.

The hacker blinked frequently during the hearing.

The Judge Mr Justice Turner told him "you are a very talented young man," and warned him: "Don't let this happen again."

Kurtaj's defence team said he found the online world a more comfortable way of interacting with other people.

"The restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests that are a core feature of ASD [autism spectrum disorder] led him to become preoccupied with the online world where he felt better able to function and exist," they said.

They said he was exposed to people who showed him how to cheat at games and then to "people who were involved in hacking".

During the pandemic, he was "very isolated" and his "connection to Lapsus$ provided him with a sense of community and self-worth that had been absent in his life previously," they added.

Kurtaj's Snapchat posts were the first sign for reporters that he had been released from a secure hospital

items.title: Java4Shell Vulnerability: Update Your JetBrains IDEs, ReSharper, .NET Tools, Toolbox App, and Gateway Now
items.content:
On November 17, 2026, Oracle and the OpenJDK project released fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a memory corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of the HotSpot JVM. The issue was reported by Calif and is known as Java4Shell.

To decode Base64 faster, HotSpot uses an intrinsic routine on x86-64 CPUs that support AVX-512 VBMI. Malformed input makes this routine write past the end of a Java array and corrupt neighboring memory. The reporters demonstrated how this routine could be exploited to execute arbitrary code in several server-side Java applications. OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, along with the 21, 25, and 27 lines, are affected across Java distributions. Oracle’s Java SE 8 Performance Pack (8u511-perf and earlier) is also affected, while standard Java 8 and Java 11 builds are not.

Every JetBrains IDE bundles JetBrains Runtime, which is based on OpenJDK. All current releases that bundle JBR 17 (17.0.6 and later), 21, or 25 are affected. This includes IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, PhpStorm, GoLand, Rider, CLion, RubyMine, RustRover, DataGrip, and the JetBrains HTTP Client CLI, as well as remote development backends.

An IDE is exposed only if both of the following conditions are true: It runs on an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, such as Intel Xeon processors from Ice Lake onward, some tenth- and eleventh-generation Intel Core processors, or AMD processors based on Zen 4 or newer; and it decodes Base64 data controlled by an attacker, for example, data received from a network peer.

At the time of publication, we are not aware of this vulnerability having been exploited against JetBrains IDEs.

The updates listed below mitigate the issue by adding the -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics option to the default VM options of all JetBrains IDEs. The option turns off the vulnerable routine for every use of java.util.Base64 in the IDE process. Base64 decoding then falls back to the regular Java implementation, which may be slower. The option is accepted on every platform. The upstream fix is being integrated into JetBrains Runtime separately, and we will update this post when new runtime builds are available.

The mitigation is included in the following IDE versions:

Toolbox App needs to be updated to 3.9.2.

ReSharper needs to be updated to one of the following versions: 2026.3.0.2, 2026.2.5.1, 2026.1.5.4, 2025.3.5.4, or 2025.2.6.3.

The IDE updates and the workaround address only the vulnerability described above. We always recommend using the latest IDE version to benefit from other security updates.

For the upstream advisories and the write-up from the reporters, see:

A complete list of recently fixed security issues is available on the Fixed security issues page on the JetBrains website. You can also subscribe to receive notifications about fixes in all JetBrains products via email.

All JetBrains IDE versions that bundle JBR 17 (17.0.6 and later), 21, or 25 are affected until they are updated to the versions listed above, or until the workaround is applied. An IDE is exposed only on x86-64 hardware with AVX-512 VBMI. We recommend upgrading as soon as possible.

We are not considering backports to older IDE versions. The workaround described above prevents this issue and is compatible with them.

The remote IDE backend is an IDE process and receives the same default VM options as desktop IDE builds with the update. Remote hosts are often cloud x86-64 machines that support AVX-512 VBMI, so be sure to update the backend, or add the option to its custom VM options in the meantime.

No. After you update, the option is one of the default VM options, so the manual entry is redundant but harmless. We will remove the default option once the IDEs bundle a version of JetBrains Runtime that contains the upstream fix.

If you have any questions regarding this issue or encounter problems updating, please get in touch with the JetBrains Support team by submitting a ticket .

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.
