Three Big Advancements in Raku Numerics - Anton Antonov
items.content:
This blog post describes three big advancements in Raku’s numerical algorithms packages:

Extensible numerical integration with “Math::NIntegrate” ;

Optimization support through COIN-OR and “Math::Optimization” ; and

Quantile regression and regression workflows through “Math::QuantileRegression” and “Math::Regressionizer” .

“Big advancements” is used here in a Raku-ecosystem functionalities sense. But more generally speaking, the advancement is the increasing availability of extensible APIs, higher-level workflows, and connections between numerical algorithms.

A second theme is the role of large language models (LLMs) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents in developing numerical software. In my experience, they helped with wrappers, translations, repetitive code, and parts of the test suites. They did not replace mathematical design and numerical validation (for me, at this point).

Remark: More detailed posts on these new(er) Raku functionalities will follow in the next few months.

Remark: Here is an extended, wordier version of blog post derived via a “blog-writer” AI-agent.

Remark: With my LLM-usage explanations below, I am not trying to imply that human work remains essential for API design, numerical validation, cross-language reconciliation, and documentation. So far, I have chosen to do those myself. But I would be very interested if that kind of work can be completely outsourced to AI-agents, and the related methodological and philosophical implications.

Remark: The headline image shows regression quantiles fitted over numerical integration sampling points.

Math::NIntegrate is a Raku numerical-integration library whose main function, nintegrate , is functionally and architecturally modeled on Wolfram Language’s NIntegrate .

The important development is not simply the presence of several quadrature algorithms. An extensible framework is provided in which integration rules, strategies, regions, variable transformations, stopping criteria, and monitors can be combined. The framework has an object-oriented design and implementation which also allows user-defined integration strategies and rules to be hooked-up to it.

The package has one-dimensional rules such as Clenshaw–Curtis, Gauss–Kronrod, and Trapezoidal rules.

It also has multidimensional and composite approaches, including Cartesian, double-exponential, Monte Carlo, and quasi-Monte Carlo methods. A Cartesian rule can combine component rules across dimensions or regions.

A rule supplies an approximation scheme. A strategy controls how that rule is applied—for example, how regions are subdivided, how estimates are adapted, or how termination is monitored. A composite rule is itself made from one or more component rules.

The framework has a nesting model of specifying integration algorithm instances:

a strategy that is not a decorator has a rule; and

a composite rule, such as a Cartesian rule, has one or more component rules.

This distinction is useful because it separates numerical approximation from the control logic surrounding it.

Framework’s architecture uses object-oriented Design Patterns , including Strategy, Composite, Decorator, Template Method, Builder, Interpreter, and Abstract Factory.

The package supports multiple stopping criteria and integration monitors. Depending on the selected method, a computation may be controlled by accuracy goals, precision goals, recursion limits, region counts, or monitoring logic. User-defined rules and strategies can also be connected to the framework when they satisfy the relevant interfaces.

items.title: Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg
items.content:
Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.

I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs , to make profile-guided optimization reproducible , and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible . But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.

Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.

If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲

I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached. 1 1 All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work . Kneel before Zod!

New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?

The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep . 💤💤💤

Every rewind time starts with two numbers:

78.0 s elapsed on the VM's one CPU 47.4 s critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs 67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing

The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path : the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.

No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.

The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis . Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep .

A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis : look at where threads block, not only where they compute.

On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤

items.title: Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem
items.content:
What follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog. The talk was in Italian, in front of a Linux audience - which explains a few of the jokes.

Linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path. A journey through the BSDs, illumos and other alternative operating systems, to reflect on Open Source as an idea, a philosophy and a practice of sharing knowledge.

My name is Stefano Marinelli. I'm a sysadmin and consultant, and I run my own small company specialised in open source services and solutions. I like to call myself the "Barista" of the BSD Cafe and the illumos Cafe , online communities of people passionate about technology, open source and sharing. Today I'm not here just to talk about operating systems, but about freedom, sharing and knowledge. From free software to open source.

My first contact with the Free Software world was in 1996, when I wasn't even 17 yet. I saw a box set advertised in a magazine: "a whole operating system, for free", at a very low price. Something like 30,000 lire. Shortly before, I'd paid roughly ten times as much for the Windows 95 upgrade edition. Dismissive and without a shred of trust, I decided to order it and give it a go. I mean: who would ever write something like that... and release the source code? But six CDs for 30,000 lire... let's try. Worst case, it'll be an experience.

It was love at first shell. That terminal opened up a whole universe, and to what I already knew (commercial licences, freeware, shareware) I added the concept of Free Software. But I didn't have enough hardware to run two operating systems, so I reinstalled Windows and put it all off. Still, I started thinking. Reflecting. Studying. In 1997 I got a new PC and started using Linux - or, as I was careful to say, GNU/Linux - for everything. Except games. For those, a small Windows partition survived, though not for long.

In 1998 I enrolled in Computer Science at the University of Bologna. Even back then, it was a faculty strongly oriented towards free software. Linux in the labs. I was one of the few who, in the first year, already knew what Free Software was (not free as in price, but...freedom!) and how to use the Linux workstations. That gave me a big advantage, especially from the second year onwards. Renzo Davoli was already pushing hard in that direction. I decided that would be my path. And so it was, and I started pushing too. Windows wasn't the "enemy" to me. The imposition was. Personally, I respect rules, but not impositions. Some people followed me, others watched from a distance. I didn't care. I was widening my horizons.

In the early 2000s I also discovered the BSDs. And I convinced my parents that I needed a laser printer for "university material". In reality, I wanted to print the excellent BSD documentation. Maybe not university material, but the printed FreeBSD Handbook probably served me better than half of the theory exams I took back then. Thanks, mom and dad!

Free Software was born out of a change. In those days, code circulated freely among people. Depending on their needs, they exchanged source code, modified it and shared it again. But at some point this began to change. There's an anecdote that, while not exhaustive, gives the idea: the printer Richard Stallman was using kept jamming, and nobody got notified. He wanted to modify the software so that he'd get a notification, as he'd done with the previous printer. Back then it was common practice, but this time he was refused. "I can't share the source code. It's under NDA." In other words, he had lost control over what he was using. He even wanted to improve the program, and instead he got a refusal.

The rest is history. At least until a few years ago.

items.content:
Nuxt 4.7 is out, with around 350 commits since v4.6.4. 🎉

It's a release with something for everyone. You can try out Nitro v3, offer your app's actions to AI agents in the browser, see type errors and lint warnings right next to your runtime errors, and validate your runtime config with a schema. And it should be even faster, especially for server rendering, hydration and installs.

The biggest thing in this release is that you can now build your Nuxt 4 app with Nitro v3 ( #37101 ). Nitro v3 is what Nuxt 5 is built on, so this is a way to move your server code (and your modules) over before you upgrade Nuxt itself.

There's no config to change. Add nitro to your dependencies:

If nitro is in your package.json , Nuxt builds with Nitro v3. To go back, just remove it.

This is highly experimental . Nitro v3 is still a release candidate, and there are no guarantees. Please try it on a branch, not in production. 🙏

Do give Nitro v3 a try! On our benchmark app with about 170 pages, the same app on 4.7 served 33% more requests per second on its home page with Nitro v3 than with Nitro v2 (926 to 1,236), and 44% more on a page with 1,000 links (219 to 316), with identical HTML.

Most Nuxt 4 apps (and the modules they use) were written for Nitro v2 and h3 v1. So, on Nuxt 4, Nitro v3 runs with a compatibility layer called nitroLegacy . It keeps imports from h3 , nitropack and #imports resolving, keeps the Nitro v2 auto-imports, useRuntimeConfig(event) , event.node and the Nitro v2 hooks working, and keeps a long list of h3 v1 behaviours, from sendRedirect ending the response to the cache-control headers cached routes send.

Once things are working, turn the layer off to find the code that still depends on it:

A few things change with Nitro v3 regardless. The main one is route rules: Nitro v3 matches them with a different pattern syntax , so /blog/* now also applies to /blog/2026/hello . Nuxt warns about each rule whose meaning changes, and stops on a rule that uses more than one wildcard (like /api/*/items/** ), which you can rewrite with a named parameter ( /api/:id/items/** ). Your app matches route rules the same way as the server, so Nuxt-only route rules like appMiddleware and ssr apply to the same paths on both.

The other is imports. If your server code imported a package your app didn't depend on, Nitro v2 fell back to Nuxt's own dependencies. Nitro v3 doesn't, so nuxt dev fails with something like Cannot find package 'ufo' . Make sure every package your server code imports is in your package.json .

Read the full list of what changes with Nitro v3 on Nuxt 4.

If something breaks for you (and it might), please open an issue and mention Nitro v3. Every report helps make the move to Nuxt 5 smoother for everyone. ❤️

The most visible change is in nuxt build . Instead of printing each tool's logs one after the other, the CLI now renders the whole production build itself from a set of new build hooks ( nuxt/cli#1662 , #37194 ). Thanks to @atinux for this one. ❤️ It works the same way with every builder (Vite, webpack, Rspack, Rsbuild) and every server builder (Nitro v2, Nitro v3 and @nuxt/vite-server ):

nuxt generate shows the prerendered routes in the same way, and ends by suggesting where to deploy:

nuxt dev --https serves over HTTP/2, so the browser loads the modules of a page in parallel on a single connection, thanks to @ProgramRipper ( nuxt/cli#1694 )

you can click and scroll inside the panes of the dev panel, thanks to @Flo0806 ( nuxt/cli#1665 )

copying a URL or an error works without a system clipboard (for example over SSH, or in a container), as long as your terminal supports it ( nuxt/cli#1693 )

new nuxt module build and nuxt module prepare commands for module authors ( nuxt/cli#1687 ), paving the way for @nuxt/module-builder v2, built on tsdown with support for TypeScript 7.1 (watch this space!)

logs from Nuxt and modules stay inside the build output rather than breaking out of it ( nuxt/cli#1705 )

items.title: Lua for data representation
items.content:
my major advocacy is that lua is a very good general purpose language. this is not an opinion shared by all. lua’s major design goal was extending and embedding into existing programs. I think the simplicity and flexibility in design persued towards the end of that goal extends to make lua a very good language in general. that said, it does its job quite well as an embedding language, and one of its more interesting use cases (and actually, one of its oldest use cases) is as a data or configuration format.

lua’s syntax provides many niceties. for instance, lua has an infinite family of multiline strings: the most basic one starts with [[ and ends with ]] . however, any amount of equal signs can be put between the two square brackets: print([======[hello, world]======]) . the only way to close a [===[ is with an accompanying ]===] , not with a ]] or a ]==] , or a ]====] .

here is a function that for any string, creates the correct multiline string to represent it:

return ("[%s[%s]%s]"):format(equal_signs, str, equal_signs)

of course, you can just use string.format with %q , but multiline strings usually provide nicer looking and more compact results. these strings are very good for representing lua code as strings in other lua code.

anyway, download this file . if you want to consume massive amounts of memory and possibly crash your computer, run it in cpython. if you want to see “hello, world” printed 5 million times, run it in lua. lua’s parser is designed to handle massive files with stride, which is fairly unique and quite necessary if lua is to be used for this purpose.

design and implementation choices like these come together to suit lua for this purpose. I’ve seen 3 main styles of using lua code to represent data or configuration. I think lua manages to accomodate each of them well, and each have their appropriate use.

chunks are much like function bodies. they have return values. so, one thing that one can do is just return a big table from a lua program.

if you’re using this style, you can omit the return and then prepend it when you load the lua files. this makes any trailing statements syntactically invalid because the return statement must be the last statement in the block. keep in mind, though, that this does not prevent arbitrary code because function literals can be used instead.

return (function() arbitrary_code() end)()

trying to strip out function literals to make this technique safer is fraught and defeats the general elegance of this technique. one can fairly readily use JSON instead.

what is often missed about lua is that it’s subtly full of metaprogrammability. for instance, lua globals are just stored in a table, and which table is used can be controlled by the code itself. this table is known as the “environment”. an environment may be passed to load as an argument. the way this can be used is that you can load a chunk with an empty environment and then capture the values it sets as globals.

then, you can get a table with all the configuration as simply as this:

assert(loadfile("config.lua", "t", config))()

lua has a bit of sugar that allows you to shed the parenthesis on function calls to make them look cleaner. an imperative style is a very suitable means to represent data in lua, and it’s very powerful.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. items.title: Protests in Chicago After Google Warns Schools About Disabling AI Feature
items.content:
This story first appeared at The 74 , a nonprofit news site covering education. Sign up for free newsletters from The 74 to get more like this in your inbox.

Pushback on the use of artificial intelligence in the classroom is seeing renewed fervor after tensions flared this month between some U.S. school districts and one of the biggest tech giants in the world.

Protests popped up Wednesday in Cambridge, Massachusetts and in Chicago, where the city’s school district recently blocked student access to generative AI , which includes ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini. The backlash comes at a critical flashpoint for the future of AI in education. Google sparked an uproar earlier this month when it said that schools that ban AI won’t be able to use search because AI is so embedded in the technology.

Chicago Public Schools has yet to plan its response to Google’s announcement, but a CPS spokesperson said in a statement that the district was “actively exploring all options to independently suppress” the AI overview that appears at the top of Google searches. If CPS cannot provide students access to the search engine without its AI feature, the district will “look to other search solutions,” the spokesperson said.

The question of whether, and how, CPS could turn off Google’s AI features points to a dilemma at the core of Wednesday’s protests: determining the extent to which tech companies should be involved in public education .

About 30 people huddled together outside Google’s office in Chicago’s West Loop, shouting chants such as “Hey Google, nice try. We don’t want your Gemini.” Most of the protesters were parents and educators, but the demonstration included some students who voiced their own skepticism about whether AI is beneficial for themselves and their peers.

“We are owed lessons and feedback from the people CPS hired, people who are passionate and dedicated to making learning fun,” Reese Mackey, a 16-year-old Kenwood Academy High School junior said at the protest. “Not by a bot whose only job is to be a yes man and compile random sources from the internet for a nonsensical answer.”

If AI is so embedded into Google’s search engine, then it might be time for schools to step back and reassess whether to use Google at all, said Cassie Creswell, executive director of Illinois Families for Public Schools, which led the rally in Chicago.

“That really shouldn’t be our gateway to human knowledge, and so we need to draw a line there,” Creswell said.

In a statement to Chalkbeat, a Google spokesperson wrote that the company was taking steps to improve its search functions for classrooms, such as through piloting its “Guided Learning” feature that uses AI to walk students through a problem step-by-step rather than providing quick answers.

The conflict with Google is just the latest in a growing movement of parents, educators, and school administrators concerned about how students’ AI usage — as well as screen time generally — may negatively impact learning. Those worries have ramped up under the Trump administration, which has largely been friendly with the AI industry. The proliferation of the ever-evolving technology, in turn, has left schools scrambling to place guardrails on its usage.

“We really need real policy…not just a guidebook with suggestions that dump the burden on teachers and kids,” Creswell told reporters.

Some cities are putting stringent AI policies in place, most notably New York City under Mayor Zohran Mamdani . Just before this school year started, the city banned the use of student-facing AI, which includes chatbots, from preschool through eighth grade . Then, at the end of October, Chalkbeat obtained a list of nearly 40 products flagged by the city’s Education Department for their AI usage, such as Grammarly and Kahoot.

items.title: Introducing DocumentExtractionClient (preview): Extract documents in .NET
items.content:
A lot of the information your apps need lives in documents. Invoices, contracts, reports, forms, and slide decks arrive as PDFs, scans, images, and Office files. Getting their content and structure out is the first step for search, automation, data entry, and archiving. It’s also how AI apps get the context they need. Before a model can answer questions about a document, your app has to turn that document into something the model can work with. Until now, each parser or service came with its own SDK and object model. Moving to another tool meant rewriting the code that used the results.

Today we’re introducing a preview of DocumentExtractionClient in Microsoft.Extensions.DocumentExtraction , along with a set of starter providers in the .NET AI Community Toolkit . Whichever provider you choose, the flow is the same. You load a document, pick a provider, and extract its contents into a common structure. Providers include a PDF parser that runs in process, a vision model behind any IChatClient , and cloud services like Azure Content Understanding.

In this post, you’ll learn what document extraction is, where DocumentExtractionClient fits among the .NET AI building blocks, and how to extract your first document, swap providers, and add middleware. Then you’ll feed the results into a data ingestion pipeline with Microsoft.Extensions.DataIngestion , the foundation for context engineering, agentic workflows, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Every sample is a single C# file you can run with dotnet run . They’re all in the document extraction samples repo .

Document extraction turns a file, such as a PDF, a scanned image, or an Office document, into structured content. A document shows text on a page, but the file often doesn’t say what that text is . A heading, a table cell, and a page number can all look like ordinary characters. Extraction recovers that structure, including:

Headings and paragraphs , so you know how the document is organized.

Tables , as a grid of cells, including merged header cells.

Figures , with their position and any description the provider can produce.

Sources , the page and region each element came from, so you can cite it or highlight it later.

Getting there is harder than it sounds. Office files and many PDFs store their text digitally, so you can read it directly. Scans and photos are only pictures of pages, so they need optical character recognition (OCR). Tables have merged header cells, pages have running headers and footers, and multi-column layouts confuse a naive reading order. Different tools solve different parts of the problem. Each one returns its results in a different shape.

Structure matters wherever you use the content, especially in AI apps. Models answer better when you give them the right context, and the right context depends on structure. When you chunk a document at its headings, each chunk covers one topic. When you flatten a table into a list of words, the model can no longer tell which number belongs to which row.

DocumentExtractionClient gives you one API for document extraction in .NET, regardless of which tool does the work. Its main method, ExtractAsync , takes a stream and returns an ExtractionDocument . That’s a tree of sections that contain text, tables, and images. Each element has sources that point back to where it came from. Providers implement this abstraction, so your code works with the same result type whether a PDF parser, a vision model, or a cloud service read the document.

If you’ve used IChatClient or IEmbeddingGenerator from Microsoft.Extensions.AI , the pattern will feel familiar, with a common abstraction, interchangeable providers, and middleware you can layer on top.

The .NET AI stack is a set of libraries, organized in layers:

Your app : web, desktop, mobile, and service apps built with .NET.

Agents and tools : agents that reason and call tools.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
